title: Roof Leak Around the Chimney: How to Find a Failed Flashing, Counterflashing, or Cricket (and Why It's Usually a Pro Job)
question: I get a water stain on the ceiling near my chimney every time it rains hard. Is my chimney flashing leaking, and can I fix it myself?
summary: A leak near the chimney almost always means the flashing failed, not the chimney itself. The part most people get wrong: they smear roofing tar or caulk over the gap, which looks fixed for one season, then cracks and traps water, hiding the real problem and rotting the roof deck underneath. Chimney flashing is a two-part system (step flashing woven into the shingles, plus counterflashing set into the mortar), and a lasting repair reseats or replaces both. Because it lives at roof height, most of this work is a job for a licensed roofer, not a ladder-and-caulk weekend fix.

commonCauses.cause: Cracked or failed sealant where the counterflashing tucks into the mortar joint (the reglet)
commonCauses.quickCheck: With binoculars from the ground, look at the line where the metal cap flashing meets the brick; dried, cracked, or peeling caulk/tar there, which flakes when poked with a screwdriver, is a failed seal.

commonCauses.cause: Rusted, too-short, or missing step flashing along the chimney-to-roof joint
commonCauses.quickCheck: From a stable ladder at the eave, look for rust stains, gaps, or a spot where a metal piece is missing between the shingle courses; a hose test on that joint will usually reveal it.

commonCauses.cause: No cricket/saddle on the up-slope side of a wide chimney, so water and debris dam up behind it
commonCauses.quickCheck: Look at the high side of the chimney: if it is wider than about 30 inches and has no small peaked 'cricket' diverting water, and leaves/pine needles pile up there, that's a prime suspect.

commonCauses.cause: Counterflashing pulled loose from the mortar reglet (lost its lead wedges / lifted in wind)
commonCauses.quickCheck: Check whether the metal cap flashing has sprung away from the brick or is flapping loose instead of being tucked tight into the joint.

commonCauses.cause: Deteriorated masonry (cracked crown, spalling brick, or open mortar joints) letting water in and mimicking a flashing leak
commonCauses.quickCheck: Look for a cracked concrete crown on top, crumbling mortar, or flaking brick faces; masonry leaks stain the same area but the flashing itself will look intact.

fixes: Confirm it is the chimney and rain-driven: note whether the stain appears only during or after rain and snowmelt, then mark the interior stain with painter's tape; water runs down rafters and sheathing, so the entry point is usually up-slope of where you see it inside.

Do a safe inspection from the ground first: use binoculars to scan the flashing line, the up-slope cricket area, the crown on top, and the mortar joints. Photograph anything cracked, rusted, loose, or clogged with debris.

Only if the roof is single-story and low-slope and you are comfortable, inspect the flashing joint from a stable ladder set at the eave; do NOT walk the roof. Look for the two layers: step flashing woven into the shingles and counterflashing tucked into the mortar. If you cannot see the joint without leaning out or stepping onto the roof, stop and hand it to a roofer.

Run a hose test to pinpoint the entry: with a helper watching the ceiling inside, wet the roof low and below the chimney first for 5-10 minutes, then move up in sections (base/apron, then the step flashing, then the up-slope/cricket side). The moment it drips inside, you have found the zone. Keep the ladder and your footing dry, and if a section (usually the up-slope/cricket side) cannot be reached without getting on the roof, leave that part for the pro rather than climbing on.

As a TEMPORARY stopgap only, and only on an accessible low-slope roof, clean the joint and press self-adhesive flashing tape or a bead of compatible polyurethane/tripolymer roof sealant over an obvious cracked reglet. This buys time until a real repair; it is not the fix.

Check the masonry while you are there: a cracked crown or open mortar joints can leak just like flashing. If the metal looks fine but the brick or crown is failing, the fix is repointing or resealing the crown, not touching the flashing.

Understand what a real repair requires so you can judge quotes: a roofer lifts the shingles, installs new step flashing, cuts a fresh reglet and sets new counterflashing sealed into the mortar, and adds a cricket if the chimney is wide. Where the counterflashing sits against masonry it should be a corrosion-resistant metal (copper, lead, stainless, or coated steel); bare aluminum corrodes in wet mortar. Caulk alone is not a repair.

Get the roof dry, then deal with the inside: let the framing and drywall dry fully, check for mold and soft/rotted sheathing, and only then patch, prime with a stain-blocking primer, and repaint the ceiling.
Prevent recurrence: keep the roof, valleys, and the area behind the chimney clear of leaves and debris, and have the flashing and masonry inspected once a year.

Know when to stop: if the leak returns after a temporary patch, if flashing must be replaced or a cricket added, or if the roof is steep, high, or wet, call a licensed roofer (and a mason for masonry work).
diyVsPro: DIY is fine for the diagnosis: a ground inspection with binoculars, a hose test with a helper, clearing debris, and a small temporary sealant or flashing-tape patch, but only on a single-story, low-slope, dry roof you can reach safely from a ladder without stepping onto it. Stop and call a licensed roofer if any of these are true: you would have to walk or work on a steep, high, or wet roof; the flashing is rusted through, missing, or must be replaced; a cricket needs to be added to a wide chimney; the counterflashing must be re-cut into the mortar; the leak comes back after you reseal it; or there is active interior water, rotted sheathing, or mold. Bring in a mason for a cracked crown, spalling brick, or bad mortar. Any two-story or steep-pitch roof is a hire-it-out job, full stop.
typicalCostUSD: DIY temporary sealant or flashing tape: about $15-50. Pro reseal of existing counterflashing: roughly $300-800. Full step + counterflashing replacement: about $500-1,500, more for copper or hard access. Adding a cricket/saddle or masonry work (crown resealing, repointing): roughly $500-3,000+ depending on size, height, and materials.
timeEstimate: DIY ground inspection and hose test: 1-2 hours. Temporary patch: under an hour. Professional flashing repair: typically a half day to a full day.
safetyNote: The biggest hazard here is a fall: steep, high, or wet roofs and any second-story height are a professional job; do not walk a roof to chase a leak. If you inspect from a ladder, set it on firm level ground at a 4-to-1 angle (1 foot out for every 4 feet up), have someone hold the base, keep three points of contact, and never overreach; stay on the ladder, not the roof. If the chimney serves a gas furnace, water heater, or wood stove, a damaged or blocked flue is a carbon-monoxide risk: keep a working CO alarm and have a certified chimney sweep inspect the flue. Do not disturb old roofing cement, mastic, flashing sealant, or 'transite' (asbestos-cement) chimney/flue materials on older homes (roughly pre-1990) without asbestos testing first. Water that has been leaking breeds mold; anything larger than about 10 square feet, hidden inside walls, or from repeated intrusion needs professional remediation, not a DIY wipe-down. Roofing tar and sealants are flammable; never apply them near a hot flue surface.
toolsParts: Binoculars for a safe ground inspection
Extension ladder with a stabilizer / standoff
Headlamp or flashlight (attic and joint inspection)
Garden hose for the section-by-section leak test
Moisture meter to confirm wet framing and track drying
Painter's tape to mark the interior stain
Compatible polyurethane or tripolymer roof/flashing sealant
Putty knife and wire brush to clean the joint
Stain-blocking primer for the ceiling repair
Phone or camera to document damage for a roofer's quote
